name: Rib cartilage rhinoplasty

angle.text: Surgeons use rib cartilage when septal cartilage is insufficient, mainly for major reconstruction and revision rhinoplasty that reshapes the nose. The result is visibly structural; evidence is limited to small surgeon series.

summary: Nose surgery that uses rib cartilage for large structural grafts, mainly in major reconstruction and revisions; evidence is limited to small surgeon series.
note: Adds a chest donor site; evidence is mainly small case series.
currentQuick:
Rib cartilage rhinoplasty uses cartilage taken from the rib to build or rebuild the nose when septal or ear cartilage is not enough, such as in major dorsal reconstruction or revisions.
The published evidence is limited to a few surgeon case series.
How it works: Carved rib cartilage supplies firm structural grafts for the nasal bridge and tip support.
Risks and caveats: It adds a donor site on the chest, and studies track graft warping and donor-site problems. Rhinoplasty revision rates are roughly 5 to 20 percent overall. It is a surgical procedure.
deepLead:
Rib cartilage rhinoplasty is nose surgery in which cartilage harvested from the patient's rib (costal cartilage) is used for structural grafts. General references note that septal cartilage is the preferred graft source and that rib or ear cartilage is used when septal cartilage is insufficient .
It is most associated with major dorsal reconstruction, revision cases and extended grafts such as the columellar strut. A retrospective cohort of 58 rib graft patients treated from 2000 to 2009 assessed graft stability, warping, need for revision and donor-site morbidity , and a later paper described anchoring an extended columellar strut with rib graft .
Published evidence is limited to a small number of surgeon case series.

name: Rhinoplasty tip-narrowing sutures

angle.text: Rhinoplasty patients with a broad or bulbous tip get sutures that reshape the cartilage without removing it, giving a narrower tip. The change is visible after healing, and published support found here is sparse.

summary: Stitches that reshape the cartilage of a wide nasal tip during rhinoplasty; sources found here are sparse.
note: Little dedicated research found; part of rhinoplasty with its general risks.
currentQuick:
Tip-narrowing sutures are stitches placed in the nose cartilage during rhinoplasty to refine a broad or bulbous tip without removing tissue.
Very little dedicated research on the technique alone was found.
How it works: The stitches pull and hold the tip cartilages in a narrower shape.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of rhinoplasty generally, including revision surgery in roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations. It is a surgical procedure.
deepLead:
Tip-narrowing sutures are stitches placed in the lower lateral cartilages of the nose during rhinoplasty to reshape and narrow a broad or bulbous tip without removing cartilage. General rhinoplasty references describe sutures as a way to narrow a wide tip by tightening the folded cartilage apex .
The sources reviewed contain little dedicated published research on the technique itself, so this article is short. Registered studies list suture-related tip work alongside grafts, but none was found specifically testing tip sutures alone.

name: Deep plane facelift

angle.text: Facelift patients seek this technique to restore a tighter jawline, fuller midface and smoother neck in one repositioned layer. The lift is visible after healing; evidence is mostly surgeon series.

summary: A facelift that lifts skin and SMAS together as one unit with ligament release for the jawline, midface and neck; evidence is mostly surgeon series.
note: Major surgery near facial nerve branches; nerve injury and hematoma are reported risks.
currentQuick:
A deep plane facelift is a surgical facelift in which the surgeon lifts the skin and the underlying SMAS layer together as one unit after releasing ligaments that hold the face in place. It targets the midface, jawline and neck.
The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, plus a few comparative studies.
How it works: Releasing retaining ligaments lets the composite flap be repositioned to lift and volumize the midface and jaw, with less reliance on skin tension.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers) and scarring. Some surgeons consider sub-SMAS dissection to carry a higher facial nerve risk. It is major surgery.
deepLead:
A deep plane facelift is a facelift technique in which the surgeon dissects beneath the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and repositions the skin and SMAS together as a single composite flap. Descriptions of the extended version emphasize release of facial retaining ligaments so the flap can be moved to volumize the midface and the jawline .
It is used for midface, jawline and neck rejuvenation. General references describe it as reducing reliance on skin tension but as technically more demanding because the dissection lies close to facial nerve branches .
Published evidence is mainly surgeon case series, comparative studies and technique papers. One study with 75 patients used objective apparent-age assessment after facial rejuvenation surgery including deep-plane facelift .

name: SMAS plication facelift

angle.text: Patients choose this less invasive facelift for a moderate tightening of the lower face and jawline. The lift is visible after healing, with less mobilisation than deep plane or SMAS flap techniques.

summary: A facelift that folds and sutures the SMAS layer for a limited lift; less invasive than deep plane, with moderate effect.
note: Facelift surgery risks include hematoma and nerve injury; comparative evidence is from surgeon studies.
currentQuick:
SMAS plication tightens the layer under the facial skin by folding and stitching it rather than cutting and moving it. It is used for cheeks, jowls and the neck line.
General references describe it as less invasive than deep-plane facelift but with more limited lifting.
How it works: Sutured folds in the SMAS pull the deeper facial tissue into a tighter position, and the skin is then redraped.
Risks and caveats: Facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion. A meta-analysis found sub-SMAS techniques considered to have a higher complication profile than less invasive SMAS techniques. It is surgery.
deepLead:
SMAS plication is a facelift approach in which the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer beneath the facial skin, is folded and sutured to tighten it, with little or no extensive dissection of the layer. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening and being less invasive, but with limited mobilization compared with SMAS flap or deep-plane techniques .
Variants described in the literature include lateral SMASectomy with plication and short-scar facelifts , anterior SMAS plication for prominent nasomandibular folds , and platysma-SMAS plication . A study of the face's retaining ligaments also described ligament correction with SMAS plication .
Evidence consists mainly of surgeon series and comparative studies, including several comparing plication with deep-plane facelift .

name: Composite facelift

chain: Midface and lower lid junction raised
angle.text: Facelift patients use this deep technique to lift sagging midface and smooth the lower eyelid to cheek junction for a more youthful look. The change is visible after healing; evidence is at surgeon-series level.

summary: A deep facelift that lifts skin, SMAS and the orbicularis muscle as one unit, reaching up to the lower eyelid and cheek junction; evidence is surgeon-series level.
note: Major surgery with deeper dissection near facial nerve branches; published evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique descriptions.
currentQuick:
The composite facelift is a surgical facelift technique in which the skin, the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the orbicularis oculi muscle around the eye are raised and repositioned together. It extends the lift into the midface and lower eyelid area, which standard lower-face lifts do not usually reach.
Published support consists mainly of surgeon-authored technique descriptions and case series. Comparative trials against other facelift methods were not found in the available literature.
How it works: Dissection goes beneath the SMAS so that skin and deeper tissue move as a single flap. Proponents describe pairing an upward-and-outward pull on the lower face with an upward-and-inward pull on the cheek and lower eyelid region to balance the result.
Risks and caveats: As with other facelifts, documented complications include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and skin necrosis, with smoking raising risk. Deeper planes bring dissection closer to facial nerve branches. It is performed by licensed surgeons under anesthesia.
deepLead:
The composite facelift is a surgical rhytidectomy technique that elevates the skin, the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) and the orbicularis oculi muscle together, extending into the periorbital region to address descent of the midface and the lower eyelid to cheek junction. It is described as a modification of the deep-plane facelift.
A 2008 surgical review describes the technique as a comprehensive approach that repositions essentially every deep structure of the aging face, including the neck, lower face, midface and lower eyelid junction, and forehead, balancing a superior-lateral vector in the lower face with a superior-medial vector in the cheek and lower eyelid. The same source states that patients with stigmata of a previous facelift, such as a lateral sweep or hollow eyes, may be corrected with it.
Published evidence consists mainly of surgeons' descriptions of their own technique and small series, including a report on esthetic outcomes after facial soft-tissue reconstruction using deep dissection and composite facelift technique. No randomized trial comparing it with other facelift approaches was found. In looksmaxxing communities it falls under hardmaxxing, meaning surgical intervention.

name: Subperiosteal facelift

angle.text: Patients seek this midface lift, often done endoscopically, to raise sagging cheeks and soften deep nasolabial folds. The lift is visible after healing and is documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.

summary: A midface lift done beneath the periosteum, often endoscopically, that repositions cheek tissue vertically; documented mainly in surgeon series from the 1990s onward.
note: Wikipedia notes longer postoperative swelling; nerve anatomy around the cheekbone and temple is a recognized surgical concern.
currentQuick:
A subperiosteal facelift frees the soft tissue of the cheek and midface from the facial bones by working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering bone. The tissue is then repositioned, mainly in an upward direction, to address flattened cheeks and deep nasolabial folds.
Surgeons in the 1990s described open and endoscopic versions, with the endoscopic approach using small incisions hidden in the hair. Available evidence is surgeon-reported series rather than randomized trials.
How it works: Dissection lifts soft tissue off bone so the whole mask of the face can be moved as a unit and fixed higher. Endoscopes let surgeons see the deep plane through short incisions.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia states the technique causes longer postoperative swelling than some alternatives. Anatomical studies highlight nerves in the cheekbone and temple region, such as the zygomaticotemporal nerve, whose injury can cause numbness or pain. General facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury and scarring.
deepLead:
A subperiosteal facelift is a surgical technique in which the soft tissues of the face are lifted completely off the underlying bone by dissecting beneath the periosteum, then repositioned. It is used to address deep nasolabial folds and sagging cheeks and is often combined with other techniques.
A 1995 report by endoscopic surgeons describes it as particularly suited to remodeling the central third of the face, and states that the endoscope allows upper-face or total-face rejuvenation without incisional scars, while making deep dissection safer and more accurate. A companion 1995 article describes open and endoscopic approaches and states the endoscopic procedure alone is indicated for mild aging (grade I rhytidosis), and in men with alopecia in whom a coronal incision is a problem, where it may be combined with neck surgery.
Evidence consists of surgeon-reported series and anatomical studies; no randomized comparison with other facelifts was found. In looksmaxxing communities it belongs to hardmaxxing, in discussions of midface and cheek restructuring.

name: Mini facelift (S-lift)

angle.text: Patients with deep nasolabial folds and sagging but a firm neck choose this short-scar lift for lighter downtime and a tighter lower face. The change is visible after healing, though Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.

summary: A short-scar facelift using small incisions near the ear, usually without neck work; lighter recovery, and Wikipedia describes the result as more temporary.
note: Suited by surgeons' accounts to early laxity; evidence is surgeon series, with few head-to-head comparisons.
currentQuick:
The mini facelift, often called the S-lift or short-scar facelift, uses shorter incisions around the ear than a traditional facelift and generally omits neck lifting. It is described as suiting people with early jowling or modest sagging and a firm neck.
Surgeons describe less dramatic change and shorter recovery. Wikipedia describes the effect as more temporary than full facelifts. A 2007 review noted that studies comparing facelift methods are few.
How it works: The S-lift suspends sagging tissue using a strong permanent purse-string suture and a short skin flap, with incisions in front of and below the ear shaped like an S.
Risks and caveats: Facelift risks in general include hematoma, nerve injury, scarring and hair loss at incisions. Combining the S-lift with laser resurfacing has been reported in retrospective series with side effect profiles described by authors.
deepLead:
The mini facelift is a family of short-scar rhytidectomy techniques, commonly called the S-lift, that use limited incisions and omit the neck lift. Wikipedia says it suits people with deep nasolabial folds and sagging but a firm, well-contoured neck, has less downtime, and may be done endoscopically; it describes the result as more temporary.
An S-lift was described in the literature in 1999 and is based on suspending sagging facial features with a strong permanent purse-string suture, according to the authors of a 2002 paper who then proposed a modification, the minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift. A 2001 dermatologic surgery paper describes an S-lift using U-suture and O-suture combined with skin resurfacing, suggesting it may help minor jowling or submental laxity in early ptosis or revision facelifts.
Reports are mainly surgeon-authored. A 2007 review of facelift techniques noted that few studies compare results between methods.

name: MACS lift

chain: Vertical lift of lower and midface
angle.text: Patients choose this short-scar lift for a vertical lift of the lower and midface with quicker recovery under local anesthesia. The tightening is visible after healing, and recovery claims come from the authors' surgeon series.

summary: A short-scar facelift that hangs the lower and mid face from above with purse-string sutures along a purely vertical vector; surgeon series report quicker recovery.
note: Evidence is mostly from the surgeons who developed and promote it; limits are discussed for the lower face and neck.
currentQuick:
The MACS (minimal access cranial suspension) lift is a short-scar facelift that uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue upward with permanent purse-string sutures anchored to firm tissue above. It was proposed in 2002 as a modification of the S-lift.
Its developers report operating times of about 2 to 2.5 hours under local anesthesia and a quicker recovery than classic facelifts, with results they describe as comparably stable. Independent reviews have discussed advantages and limitations.
How it works: Purse-string sutures lift the neck and lower face along a vertical vector with no lateral tension; an optional third, malar suture adds midface correction in the extended version.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia says less skin is raised, so bleeding and nerve-injury risk are lower than with traditional facelifts, but general facelift risks still apply, including hematoma, scarring and nerve injury. Reviews have outlined limitations for the lower third of the face.
deepLead:
The minimal access cranial suspension (MACS) lift is a short-scar rhytidectomy for the lower and middle third of the face that uses a vertical vector, involves no lateral tension, and in its authors' description can be performed under local anesthesia in 2 to 2.5 hours. It was proposed in 2002 as a modified version of the S-lift, suspending tissue with purse-string sutures.
Wikipedia states that the MACS lift uses a short incision in front of the ear and suspends sagging tissue vertically from above, raises less skin so bleeding and nerve injury risk is lower, takes about 2.5 hours against 3.5 for a traditional facelift, and has a recovery of 2 to 3 weeks versus 3 to 4. The developers write that it reduces recovery time and morbidity and that results are as stable as more classic, extended techniques.
It exists in a simple version with two purse-string sutures for the neck and lower face and an extended version that adds a third, malar suture for the midface. The literature is dominated by surgeons who use the technique; independent assessments exist, including one examining its advantages and limitations.

name: APTOS thread lift

angle.text: Patients use these barbed threads as a non-surgical way to lift sagging facial tissue. Early series, including 186 patients, reported improved contour, while case reports describe thread migration and expulsion.

summary: A non-surgical lift using barbed non-absorbable threads placed under the skin; early series report improvement, while case reports document migration and expulsion.
note: Wikipedia cites a BBC investigation reporting short training courses for practitioners; complications such as thread migration have been reported.
currentQuick:
APTOS threads are barbed polypropylene sutures inserted under facial skin to support sagging tissue without a surgical facelift. They are typically promoted for the cheeks, jowls and jawline and form part of the broader thread-lift category.
Early reports from the originator's group describe improvement in contour in a series of 186 patients. Later literature includes case reports of complications and small retrospective studies of combined treatments.
How it works: Sharp dents or barbs along each thread grip the tissue; the thread is anchored so that it holds the tissue in a higher position. Some authors describe stimulating tissue response around the thread as well.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include thread migration and partial expulsion; a MACS facelift has been used to correct APTOS complications. Wikipedia notes that UK practitioners face no mandatory qualification and cites a physician quoted by the BBC describing thread lifts as potentially causing irreversible damage.
deepLead:
APTOS threads are barbed non-absorbable sutures, originally made of polypropylene with dents along their length, used to lift ptotic facial tissue without a facelift. The technique was described in 2002 by a group who used them in 186 patients and reported success in lifting various areas and improving facial contour.
A 2004 review describes self-retaining barbed sutures as innovations for nonsurgical facial and neck rejuvenation available as short APTOS threads or long WOFFLES threads; its author uses APTOS for malar rounding and firming and WOFFLES as a sling to temporal scalp tissue. A 2005 chapter describes the approach as the featherlift.
Complications are documented in case literature, including thread migration and partial expulsion. Wikipedia notes that UK aesthetic practitioners need no mandatory qualification and reports a BBC investigation of short low-cost training courses. Evidence is mainly case series and retrospective studies, plus small registered trials without published results found.

name: Lower facelift with neck lift

angle.text: Patients combine jowl lifting with platysma and fat work to define the jawline and neck together. The result is visible after healing; the literature is surgeon-reported with limited comparative data.

summary: A combined jowl-and-neck lift, often adding platysma work and fat removal to the facelift; literature is surgeon-reported with limited comparative data.
note: Major surgery; Wikipedia lists hematoma and nerve injury as principal complications of facelifts.
currentQuick:
A lower facelift with neck lift targets jowls, the jawline and the neck together. It typically tightens deeper layers (the SMAS), may tighten the platysma muscle band of the neck, removes or contours fat under the chin, and trims and redrapes skin.
Published reports are mostly from surgeons describing their combined techniques, including one team that argues combinations of methods are essential for lasting results. Registered trials include comparisons of office-based limited and hospital-based full facelifts.
How it works: Facelift tightening of SMAS or deep-plane tissue lifts the jowls, while platysma work, submental lipectomy and sometimes chin implants reshape the neck and under-chin contour.
Risks and caveats: Facelift complications documented include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and hair loss; smoking raises the risk. Wikipedia notes the greater auricular nerve is the most frequently injured sensory nerve.
deepLead:
A lower facelift with neck lift is a combined surgical approach to the jowls, jawline and neck, in which facelift tightening of the SMAS or deeper tissues is performed together with treatment of neck structures such as the platysma muscle and submental fat. Wikipedia notes that a traditional facelift addresses neck skin and platysma laxity.
A 1983 anatomical and clinical report from nearly 100 patients described anterior neck principles combining submandibular lipectomy, excision of the submental fat pad, chin implantation, creation or tightening of a platysma muscular sling, and skin tightening or resection. A 2018 team's lower face and neck rejuvenation combined method uses liposuction, lipectomy, myotomies, suspensions and tissue-induction techniques, arguing that combinations are essential for satisfactory lasting results.
Other surgeons report SMAS plication with periauricular purse-string and malar fat pad elevation evaluated with FACE-Q, and endoscopic deep plane facelifts with a classification for patient selection. Evidence is mostly case series.

name: Skin-only facelift

angle.text: Users consider it the simplest facelift, with milder recovery, for tightening loose facial skin and softening jowls and sagging. The skin tightening is visible once healed. The surgical literature compares it with deeper SMAS and deep-plane techniques, which are described as longer-lasting.

summary: Lifting and trimming just the skin of the face; the oldest, simplest facelift, with milder recovery and a shorter-lived result than deeper techniques.
note: Surgical procedure; reported longevity figures come from summaries, not controlled trials.
currentQuick:
A skin-only facelift lifts the facial skin and removes the excess without working on the SMAS or muscle underneath. It was the standard facelift for most of the early 20th century and remains described as a simpler option for mild jowling.
Encyclopedia summaries say it has fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper facelifts, but results are reported to last around 5 to 10 years. No dedicated trials were found.
How it works: The surgeon raises a skin flap, pulls it in a chosen direction, trims the surplus and closes the incision, relying on the skin itself to hold the result [1].
Risks and caveats: General facelift risks include haematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and infection; smoking, hypertension and diabetes raise risk. Skin-only technique is described as having fewer complications than deeper variants, but excessive skin tension can distort the ears or give a windswept look [1].
deepLead:
A skin-only facelift is a form of rhytidectomy in which the surgeon lifts and redrapes the facial skin and removes the excess, without separately tightening or repositioning the deeper tissue layers such as the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) or facial muscles . It is the older, simpler approach to facelifting and is contrasted in the surgical literature with SMAS, deep-plane and composite techniques .
Descriptions of the technique say it carries fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper procedures, and that it may be suited to a simple jowl lift in patients in their 30s and 40s . The same reference reports that skin-only results may last roughly 5 to 10 years, with some patients seeking a touch-up sooner . No clinical trials of the technique specifically are present in the sources reviewed for this article, and the longevity figures come from an encyclopedia summary rather than from controlled studies.

name: Upper blepharoplasty

chain: Excess lid skin and fat removed
angle.text: Used to remove hooded or drooping upper-lid skin so the eyes look more open and rested, with the scar hidden in the natural crease. The visible change is the surgical result itself. Evidence for appearance outcomes is mostly surgeon-reported.

summary: Removing excess upper-lid skin, muscle and fat through a crease incision; established surgery for hooding, with mostly surgeon-reported evidence.
note: Surgical procedure; dry eye and eyelid malposition are recognised concerns.
currentQuick:
Upper blepharoplasty trims loose skin, muscle and sometimes fat from the upper eyelids through an incision hidden in the natural crease. It is done both to clear skin that blocks vision and to reduce a hooded or tired look.
The literature is mostly technique reports and case series, with a few randomised comparisons and an evidence-based review.
How it works: Redundant tissue is excised along a marked ellipse in the lid crease, and the incision is closed with sutures or tissue glue. It may be paired with brow lifting or ptosis repair [5][7].
Risks and caveats: Swelling and bruising are common for several weeks [3]. Surgeons screen for dry eye, thyroid eye disease, bleeding disorders and body dysmorphic disorder beforehand [4]. Registered studies are examining dry eye and vision changes after the operation [11][12].
deepLead:
Upper blepharoplasty is surgery on the upper eyelids that removes or repositions excess skin, orbicularis oculi muscle and sometimes fat . The incision is placed in the natural eyelid crease so that the scar is concealed . It is performed for functional reasons, such as excess skin (dermatochalasis) obstructing the upper visual field, and for cosmetic reasons, such as hooded or tired-looking lids .
The procedure is often combined with brow lifting or ptosis repair . Published research includes surgical technique papers, randomised comparisons of wound closure methods , a 2014 evidence-based review , and a study of how rejuvenation surgery affects how attractive, feminine and approachable faces are perceived . A number of registered trials are studying outcomes such as dry eye, vision quality and patient-reported satisfaction .

name: Fat repositioning (tear trough)

angle.text: Users choose it to soften under-eye bags and the tear trough hollow together by relocating fat instead of removing it. The smoother lower lid is visible after healing. Support comes from surgeon case series rather than randomised trials.

summary: Moving under-eye fat into the tear trough instead of cutting it out; documented in surgeon case series, not randomised trials.
note: Surgical procedure; evidence is retrospective case series.
currentQuick:
Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgery that shifts the fat pads responsible for under-eye bags down over the bony rim to fill the tear trough hollow, instead of removing them.
Published evidence consists of surgeon-reported case series of 66, 97 and 232 patients. No randomised trials were found.
How it works: Orbital fat is released and redistributed over the infraorbital rim through an incision inside the lower lid or just under the lashes, sometimes secured with fixation sutures [1][3].
Risks and caveats: Lower-eyelid surgery can cause eyelid malposition and other complications; surgeons sometimes add a canthopexy to reduce that risk [1]. Procedure-specific complication data are not summarised in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgical technique in which orbital fat that would otherwise bulge as an under-eye bag is mobilised and moved over the infraorbital rim to fill the hollow below it, known as the tear trough . It contrasts with traditional lower blepharoplasty, in which herniated fat is simply removed.
The approach is reported in the plastic surgery literature through case series, including a 66-patient series of transconjunctival repositioning in the sub-orbicularis oculi fat (intra-SOOF) plane , a 97-patient cohort studying external fixation of the moved fat in transcutaneous surgery , and a 232-patient series asking whether visibly herniated fat is needed for the procedure to be performed . Evidence is limited to such surgeon-reported series; the sources reviewed contain no randomised trial.

name: CO2 laser blepharoplasty

angle.text: Promoted as a way to get the same eyelid reshaping with a laser, sometimes combined with resurfacing of fine wrinkles around the eyes. Small studies report less bleeding and bruising during recovery, with a similar final look.

summary: Eyelid surgery with a CO2 laser instead of a scalpel; small studies report less bleeding and bruising but the same final look.
note: Surgical procedure; rare serious infections reported.
currentQuick:
CO2 laser blepharoplasty uses a carbon dioxide laser to cut and seal small vessels during eyelid surgery. It can be paired with laser resurfacing of wrinkled eyelid skin.
Small paired comparisons from the 1980s and 1990s report less bleeding, bruising and swelling on the laser side, with no long-term difference in cosmetic result.
How it works: The laser vaporises tissue while coagulating small blood vessels, giving a drier surgical field than a scalpel [2].
Risks and caveats: General blepharoplasty risks apply. Published reports include a case of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty and cases of strabismus after cosmetic blepharoplasty [6][10].
deepLead:
CO2 laser blepharoplasty is eyelid surgery in which a carbon dioxide laser is used as the cutting and coagulating instrument in place of a cold steel scalpel and electrocautery . It may be combined with laser resurfacing of the surrounding skin to treat periocular wrinkles .
Published reports from the 1980s and 1990s, mostly small series and paired side-by-side comparisons, describe less intraoperative bleeding and less early bruising and swelling with the laser, but report no long-term difference in cosmetic result or scarring compared with conventional technique . Documented complications include a case report of necrotising fasciitis after laser blepharoplasty .

name: Double eyelid suture (non-incisional)

chain: Sutures bind lid skin to deeper tissue
angle.text: Used mainly by people who lack an upper-lid crease to create a double eyelid without an incision, with a quick procedure. The new crease is visible straight away. Reports describe the crease sometimes fading over time.

summary: Stitch-only creation of an upper eyelid crease; fast and incision-free, but the crease can fade and buried sutures can injure the eye.
note: Retrospective data only; suture exposure and corneal injury are documented complications.
currentQuick:
The non-incisional double eyelid method uses buried stitches instead of a cut to form a crease in the upper lid. It is a common East Asian aesthetic procedure and is described as quicker than the incisional approach.
Published work is retrospective: large cohorts on crease loss and reoperation, plus case series on suture complications. No randomised trials were found.
How it works: Sutures passed through the lid bind the skin to deeper tissue, so that a fold forms when the eye opens [1].
Risks and caveats: The crease may fade or loosen, requiring reoperation [12][13]. Buried or exposed sutures can irritate or injure the cornea and have required removal [2][3][4].
deepLead:
Non-incisional double eyelid surgery, also called the buried-suture or suture-ligation method, creates an upper eyelid crease by passing sutures through the lid to bind the skin to deeper tissue such as the levator aponeurosis, without removing skin through an incision . It is a variant of East Asian blepharoplasty, aimed at people who naturally lack a supratarsal crease .
Encyclopedia summaries say the method is quicker and associated with fewer complications than the incisional approach but that the crease can be static and may fade . The published literature is largely retrospective and focuses on complications of the buried thread, such as suture exposure and corneal injury, and on crease loss and reoperation .

name: Le Fort I osteotomy

angle.text: A major jaw operation used to correct bite and upper-jaw position, and discussed in looksmaxxing circles for reshaping the midface. Moving the maxilla visibly changes projection and proportion. It has a large clinical literature, mostly on function rather than looks.

summary: Cutting and repositioning the upper jaw to fix bite and midface proportion; major surgery with a large clinical literature.
note: Major jaw surgery with bleeding, nerve and necrosis risks.
currentQuick:
Le Fort I osteotomy cuts the upper jaw free through the mouth, moves it up, forward or down, and fixes it with plates. It is used for bite problems, long-face deformity, cleft-related deficiency and sleep apnoea, and also changes midface appearance.
The clinical literature is large but mostly observational, covering complications, stability and fixation methods.
How it works: A horizontal bone cut above the tooth roots frees the maxilla, which is repositioned and fixed, usually with titanium plates and screws [1].
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, condylar resorption and rarely aseptic necrosis of the maxilla [1][5][6]. Recovery involves weeks of restricted diet and months of bone healing [1].
deepLead:
A Le Fort I osteotomy is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the upper jaw, or maxilla, is cut horizontally above the roots of the upper teeth, freed, moved to a new position, and fixed in place, commonly with titanium plates and screws . It is used to correct bite problems and skeletal jaw discrepancies such as vertical maxillary excess, to treat cleft-related maxillary deficiency, and as part of maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea . It is also used for facial aesthetic goals, because moving the maxilla changes midface projection and proportion .
The surgical literature includes a prospective evaluation of complications in 1000 patients , reports of condylar resorption and aseptic necrosis after maxillary osteotomies , and analyses of long-term stability by direction of movement . Registered trials compare fixation plates and surgical designs . In looksmaxxing forums the operation is discussed alongside other jaw and midface procedures, sometimes with disagreement about aesthetic results .

name: T-osteotomy genioplasty (mini V-line)

angle.text: A Korean chin-bone surgery sought to narrow the chin toward a V-line shape and, in many descriptions, lengthen it. The reshaped chin is visible once swelling settles. Evidence is surgeon case reports rather than trials.

summary: Korean chin-bone surgery that narrows and slightly lengthens the chin; supported by surgeon case reports, not trials.
note: Evidence is limited to technique reports; carries general jaw-surgery risks such as lip numbness.
currentQuick:
The T-osteotomy, or mini V-line, is a chin operation in which a trapezoid of bone is removed so the chin becomes narrower, and the segment is refixed with plates. It is often discussed for people who feel the chin is wide relative to the jaw angle.
Published evidence consists of surgeon-authored technique papers and reviews; no controlled trials were found.
How it works: Through the mouth, the surgeon cuts the chin bone horizontally and vertically, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece, and repositions the segment with titanium plates, reattaching the mentalis muscle. Average lengthening of about 2-3 mm is described.
Risks and caveats: General genioplasty risks include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip numbness or weakness, and less commonly infection, bony changes and nerve damage. It is a surgical procedure performed by oral/maxillofacial or plastic surgeons.
deepLead:
T-osteotomy genioplasty, commonly called the mini V-line operation, is a chin-bone procedure that narrows the chin and, in many descriptions, lengthens it. It originated in Korean craniofacial practice. The surgeon makes one horizontal and two vertical bone cuts, removes a trapezoid-shaped piece, and repositions and fixes the remaining chin segment with titanium plates.
It is performed mainly for aesthetic reasons, particularly in patients with a chin described as disproportionately wide. A 2014 report in the Journal of Craniofacial Surgery describes narrowing the front of the mandible, including the chin, while leaving the back of the jaw untouched, for patients who do not have an excessive mandible angle. The same approach is also discussed as one of several add-on procedures in facial feminization surgery.
Evidence is limited to surgical technique reports and case series by surgeons who perform the operation; no randomized trials were found. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as one option among jaw and chin hardmaxxing procedures.

name: Surgery-first orthognathic approach

angle.text: Used by people planning corrective jaw surgery who want the facial change earlier, without a long pre-surgical braces phase. The jaw repositioning itself changes face shape. Cohort studies report treatment-time and stability findings that vary.

summary: Jaw surgery done before (or without) braces; studied in cohorts, with treatment-time and stability findings that vary by study.
note: Major jaw surgery; general orthognathic risks apply, plus planning-specific precautions.
currentQuick:
Surgery-first reorders corrective jaw surgery: the bone operation comes before, or replaces, the long pre-surgical braces phase. Surgeons using it say better 3D planning and miniscrews make this possible.
Studies, mostly cohort comparisons in class III patients, have looked at treatment time, stability, quality of life and planning accuracy.
How it works: The jaw is repositioned according to a virtual plan with a pre-set surgical bite, and orthodontic tooth movement follows afterwards, often with miniscrew assistance.
Risks and caveats: Orthognathic surgery carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection and nerve injury with numbness that is usually temporary. A 2019 review discusses precautions and complications specific to the surgery-first sequence.
deepLead:
The surgery-first orthognathic approach (SFOA) is a way of sequencing corrective jaw surgery in which the bone operation is done before, or without, the traditional period of pre-surgical orthodontic treatment with braces. Conventional orthognathic care uses braces before and after surgery, with the pre-surgical phase traditionally lasting up to about a year.
Surgeons who use the approach cite advances in 3D virtual planning and in the use of miniscrews for orthodontic control after surgery, which they say allow stable occlusion without pre-surgical tooth decompensation. Studies, mostly in skeletal class III patients from East Asia and Europe, have compared SFOA with the conventional sequence on treatment time, stability, quality of life and accuracy.
The evidence base is mainly cohort and comparative studies; the sources reviewed describe a mix of findings, including reductions in total treatment time in some series and cautions about precautions and complications. Within looksmaxxing culture it is discussed as the route by which people hoping for a faster change in facial structure pursue jaw surgery.

name: Custom PEEK jaw implant

angle.text: A made-to-fit plastic implant discussed for building up or reconstructing the jaw for a more defined contour. The added contour is visible once healed. PEEK is established in spine and skull surgery, while cosmetic jaw studies have not been located.

summary: A patient-specific jaw implant in PEEK plastic; the material is established in spine and skull surgery, but no cosmetic jaw studies were found.
note: No clinical studies of cosmetic custom PEEK jaw implants were found.
currentQuick:
A custom PEEK jaw implant is a made-to-measure implant in a rigid medical plastic, discussed as an alternative to other jaw implant materials. PEEK itself has a long record in spinal and cranial implants.
No clinical studies specific to cosmetic jaw augmentation were found.
How it works: The implant is shaped to a patient's anatomy and placed against or fixed to the jawbone. PEEK is radiolucent and, being hydrophobic, may not fully fuse with bone.
Risks and caveats: No procedure-specific risk data were found. General implant surgery risks, such as infection and implant displacement, apply to facial implants as described for chin implants.
deepLead:
A custom PEEK jaw implant is a patient-specific implant made of polyether ether ketone (PEEK), a semicrystalline thermoplastic, intended to augment or reconstruct the jaw. PEEK is used in spinal fusion devices and as a partial skull replacement in neurosurgery.
PEEK was invented in 1978 and marketed in the early 1980s by a division of ICI that later became Victrex. It is radiolucent, meaning largely transparent to X-rays, and because it is hydrophobic it may not fully fuse with bone.
No clinical study of a custom PEEK implant for cosmetic jaw augmentation was found. Registered studies involve PEEK or related polymers in dental implant frameworks and in facial plates, which are different applications.

name: Maxillary distraction osteogenesis

angle.text: A bone-stretching technique for advancing a recessed upper jaw gradually, sometimes discussed for midface projection. The advancement is visible in the face. It is studied mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases rather than cosmetic use.

summary: Gradual upper-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, studied mainly in cleft and severe hypoplasia cases rather than cosmetic use.
note: Evidence comes from cleft and deformity patients; cosmetic use in people without a deformity has not been studied.
currentQuick:
In maxillary distraction, the upper jaw is cut and then slowly pulled forward by a device so new bone forms in the gap. It is used mainly for severe upper-jaw underdevelopment such as in cleft lip and palate.
Studies compare it with conventional advancement for relapse and stability; a Cochrane review found too little evidence for general conclusions.
How it works: After a cut, a latency of about a week, and activation at roughly 1 mm per day, a consolidation period lets the new bone mature before the device is removed.
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include infection, unintended direction of bone growth, hardware failure and, in craniofacial distraction generally, nerve injury. External devices carry pin-site infection and scarring risks.
deepLead:
Maxillary distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique for advancing the upper jaw gradually. The bone is cut, a distraction device is attached, and the segments are slowly separated so new bone forms in the gap, rather than moving the jaw in one step as in conventional orthognathic surgery.
Its main published use is severe maxillary hypoplasia, especially in cleft lip and palate. Early reports from the late 1990s described rigid external devices used in children and adolescents with severe deficiency. It has also been used in combination with mandibular distraction in hemifacial microsomia.
Studies have compared it with orthognathic surgery in cleft patients for morbidity, relapse and five-year stability. A 2018 Cochrane review, as summarized by Wikipedia, found only one small study (47 participants) on maxillary distraction in cleft lip and palate, insufficient for general conclusions. In looksmaxxing contexts it is mentioned as a more extensive alternative to Le Fort I advancement.
